blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Tests of normality assess whether data are consistent with a Normal distribution. The main visual tool is the Normal quantile–quantile (Q-Q) plot: the sorted data are plotted against the values a Normal distribution would give at the same cumulative proportions. Formal tests (§9.3.1–§9.3.2) test H₀: the data come from a Normal population.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Skewness and kurtosis (recall §3.9–§3.10) summarise shape in one number each. A Q-Q plot shows where the shape departs from Normal. If the data are Normal, the points lie close to a straight line. A curve that bends away at one end shows skew; an S-shape shows tails heavier or lighter than Normal.

blocks.alt: Normal Q-Q plots of clinic weights and CBHI distances
blocks.caption: Figure 9.1. Normal Q-Q plots. Left: weights of the 100 children in the under-five clinic lie on the line. Right: distance to the nearest facility for the 500 CBHI households. The points fall below the line at the lower end: distances have a long lower tail that runs down to a floor at 0 km (24 households live within 1 km of a facility). The upper tail is shorter than Normal, so the distribution is skewed to the left.

points.html: The Q-Q plot is the primary check. It shows the kind and size of the departure, which a p-value cannot.
A formal test’s H₀ is Normality. A non-significant result does not prove Normality; it means the data could not rule it out (recall §8.5).

With small samples the tests have low power and miss real departures; with large samples they flag departures too small to matter. The t-test itself becomes less dependent on Normality as n grows (recall §6.6). Use the plot and the size of the sample together, not the p-value alone.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The Shapiro–Wilk test measures how closely the sorted sample follows the pattern expected from a Normal sample. Its statistic W lies between 0 and 1; values near 1 are consistent with Normality.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: W is closely related to the squared correlation between the sorted data and the ideal Normal scores: a numerical version of how straight the Q-Q plot is. A small p-value says the plot bends more than chance would explain.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
shapiro.test(cl$weight_kg)
shapiro.test(cb$distance_km)
    Shapiro-Wilk normality test
data:  cl$weight_kg
W = 0.99212, p-value = 0.8299

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test
data:  cb$distance_km
W = 0.96269, p-value = 5.953e-10

Clinic weights: W = 0.992, p = 0.83, no evidence against Normality, matching the straight Q-Q plot. CBHI distances: W = 0.963 is still close to 1, but with n = 500 even this departure gives p < 0.001. The plot shows it comes from the long lower tail and the floor at 0 km. For a comparison of mean distance between two groups of this size, the Central Limit Theorem makes a t-test adequate despite the tiny p-value.

points.html: In a simulation comparison, “Shapiro-Wilk test is the most powerful normality test, followed by Anderson-Darling test, Lilliefors test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test”, but “the power of all four tests is still low for small sample size” (Razali & Wah, 2011).
A small p-value with a large n often means a trivial departure (the CBHI example). Look at the plot.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The Kolmogorov–Smirnov (K-S) test compares the sample’s cumulative distribution with a fully specified theoretical cumulative distribution, using the largest vertical gap between the two curves (recall the ogive, §4.3.3).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: K-S is a general goodness-of-fit test for any continuous distribution; testing Normality is one use. Its catch: the comparison distribution must be fully specified in advance. The NIST/SEMATECH handbook calls this “perhaps the most serious limitation … if location, scale, and shape parameters are estimated from the data, the critical region of the K-S test is no longer valid”, and adds that the test “tends to be more sensitive near the center of the distribution than at the tails”.

points.html: When the mean and SD are estimated from the same sample, the usual situation, the Lilliefors correction gives valid p-values.
For testing Normality, K-S is less powerful than Shapiro–Wilk (Razali & Wah, 2011). Prefer the Q-Q plot plus Shapiro–Wilk.
